summary: Butterfly metrology is experimentally demonstrated on a superconducting quantum processor using information scrambling to achieve quantum-enhanced phase sensing with sensitivity approaching $N/2$ of the Heisenberg limit for up to 10 qubits. The protocol establishes genuine multipartite entanglement dynamically through many-body evolution, directly connecting information scrambling measured via out-of-time-order correlators to sensing performance.
motivation: Existing quantum sensing protocols require preparation of complex entangled states or precise Hamiltonian engineering, limiting scalability; scrambling-based approaches offer a universal and scalable alternative that generates entanglement dynamically through many-body interactions.
method: A butterfly state is prepared via time-reversal sequences with tunable XX+YY coupling ($J \approx 2\pi \times 3$ MHz) between nearest-neighbor qubits on a 16-qubit superconducting processor, with phase encoding in $e^{-i\phi S_z}$ and readout via Fisher information extraction from $\langle\sigma_x\rangle(\phi)$ measurements; genuine multipartite entanglement is characterized via full state tomography and out-of-time-order correlators measured with $\sim 99.8\%$ single-qubit fidelity.
result: Inverted sensitivity $\eta^{-1}$ exceeds the standard quantum limit $N$ and saturates near the predicted $N/2$ after normalization, with slopes in $\langle\sigma_x\rangle$ increasing from $-2.97$ to $-4.83$ for $N=6,8,10$; genuine multipartite entanglement concurrence peaks ($C_{\mathrm{GME}} \approx 0.1$ for 6 qubits) at $t=56$ ns coinciding with maximal sensitivity, demonstrating sensitivity directly scales with scrambling-induced entanglement buildup.
